title: The 8 Fallacies of Distributed Computing
description: Peter Deutsch's eight false assumptions that every developer makes about distributed systems, each illustrated with real-world disasters.

segments.text: In 1994, Peter Deutsch at Sun Microsystems wrote down eight assumptions that developers new to distributed systems always make. Every single one is wrong. And every single one has caused real outages.

Fallacy one: the network is reliable. It's not. Packets get dropped, cables get cut, switches fail. In 2017, an Amazon S3 outage took down half the internet because a single network command was mistyped.

Fallacy two: latency is zero. Every network call takes time. A function call takes nanoseconds. A network call across data centers? Tens of milliseconds. That's a million times slower. Treat them the same and your system crawls.

Fallacy three: bandwidth is infinite. It's not. In 2020, the global shift to remote work caused bandwidth saturation across multiple ISPs. Streaming services had to reduce video quality to keep the internet functional.
Fallacy four: the network is secure. Every packet crosses untrusted territory. The 2013 Target breach started from an HVAC vendor's network access. Assume every network boundary can be compromised.
segments.thought_prompt: How many network boundaries does a single API call cross in a microservices architecture?

segments.text: Fallacy five: topology doesn't change. Servers come and go. Cloud instances are ephemeral. Auto-scaling adds and removes nodes constantly. If your code hardcodes IP addresses, you're already broken.

Fallacy six: there is one administrator. In reality, dozens of teams manage different parts of the network. A DNS change by one team can cascade into failures for another. Nobody has the full picture.

Fallacy seven: transport cost is zero. Serialization, deserialization, encryption, compression — every network call has overhead. Google found that Protobuf serialization alone consumed significant CPU across their fleet.

Fallacy eight: the network is homogeneous. Your system will talk to services using different protocols, different versions, different operating systems. The real world is messy, and your architecture must handle that mess.
Notice the pattern? Every fallacy assumes the network behaves like a local system. It doesn't. Distributed computing is fundamentally different from single-machine programming.
segments.thought_prompt: Which of these fallacies have you unknowingly assumed in your own code?

segments.text: The good news? Once you internalize these fallacies, you design differently. You add retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation. You build for failure because failure is the norm, not the exception.
